title: The Lord ruleth me (Psalm 22 [23])
hookLine: green pastures, still waters, and the valley of the shadow

cards: A funeral Mass, a hospital bedside, a film where a soldier waits for dawn: this psalm turns up in all of them, and plenty of people who have never opened a Bible can say its first line. The Lord is my shepherd.

But open the Douay-Rheims, the Bible English-speaking Catholics used for generations, and it starts with different words. Same psalm, same care, but a different first verb, and it changes the picture.

teach.b: It's Psalm 22 in the Douay, 23 in most Bibles: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing." Ruleth, because the Douay follows the Latin, Dominus regit me, the Lord guides me, steers me.
The Hebrew says, more simply, the Lord is my shepherd. Both are about the same care: someone who knows the way and leads. Then the well-known pictures.
"He hath set me in a place of pasture. He hath brought me up, on the water of refreshment." A place to drink and rest.
Then the dark part, which the psalm doesn't skip: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me."
The shepherd doesn't lead around the valley. He leads through it. And the grammar changes: until now the psalm talks about God, he, he, he.
In the valley it talks to God: thou art with me.
Then a table set before enemies, a head anointed with oil, and a cup: "my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it!" Some early Christians heard the sacraments here.
Ambrose, bishop of Milan, connected it with the newly baptized at Easter: the water of refreshment was the font, the oil was the anointing, the table and the chalice were their first Eucharist.
It ends with goodness and mercy following all the days of life, and a home in the house of the Lord.

how: Catholics often hear Psalm 22 [23] at funeral Masses and on Good Shepherd Sunday, and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; many know it by heart and pray it at bedsides.

o: someone who knows the way and leads the flock
a strict ruler who punishes those who stray
a hired hand who simply counts the sheep

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: a place to drink and rest

s: the Douay-Rheims opens the Lord is my shepherd
it opens the Lord ruleth me, following the Latin Dominus regit me.
in the valley, the psalm starts speaking to God directly
he, he, he becomes thou art with me.
the psalm promises the shepherd will avoid the dark valley
he leads through it: I will fear no evils, for thou art with me.

games.q: you're a sheep, and the path runs straight into a dark valley. what does the psalm say the shepherd does?
o: finds a way around the valley.
leads you through it, and stays with you.
leaves you to find your own way.
games.why: though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. through, not around.

practice: Pray the psalm slowly; it's about six verses, so read it at half speed, or walk through its pictures in your mind: a pasture, still water, a dark valley, a table, oil, a full cup, a house.
Stop at the picture that fits your life right now: are you at the water, or in the valley? If you pray, say to God there, thou art with me; if you don't, just notice where you are.

wordCard.voice: Shepherd. The Hebrew word behind the Douay's ruleth me, someone who knows the way leads me, even through the valley. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my shepherd. where the Latin and the Douay have ruleth me, the Hebrew has the Lord is my shepherd.

carryVoice: Your line: I shall want nothing. The shepherd knows the way. That's day one hundred sixty-three.
